PRO-TYPISTS, INC.

: -- first interview with Jack Butler, 65 2nd Avenue, New York, New York. It's January 27th, Saturday, at his home.
Now, Mr. Butler?
Yes.
: Do you recall -- we'd like to deal with your childhood now. When and where were you born and what do you know about your family line? That is, whether Indian, Scotch, Irish (inaudible)?

Well, I was born in Washington. The District of Columbia, it was called, in 1909. I was born in an area called Foggy Bottom. It was called Foggy Bottom because when they built Lincoln's tomb, they forgot -- neglected so that frogs (inaudible) and it seems that the river would overflow, you'd have Avenue A, B, C and D and E -- in fact, they were called streets, and in the wintertime -- A Street didn't exist. B Street didn't exist. It would come as far as C, and I lived on E. And the school was right across the street from me, Briggs School. My mother, she said that circumstances of being born was that I was born with a veil or enveloped and it seems that if you (inaudible), you are (inaudible).
My mother was a very, very, very wonderful person. She was from Lafayette, Louisiana. Her family name was

Lefebvre. This is a mixture of Negro and Indian, although I saw many blanché or fair-haired people coming up to visit us and they were kissing mother. So I would -- they was cousins or something of this sort.

My father, it seems, that I heard of him but I didn't see him until I was 50 years old and very rare occasion. It seems that my mother was working in service naturally for certain people who had the money and they fell in love or something happened there and I was created -- I happened on the scene. So as I can remember, my mother was telling me, "Your father is in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. You don't look like your father. You look like your uncle." So I kept that in mind. And then when I was about (inaudible), I remember vaguely that I must have been (unintelligible) something green in color above me and I was reaching up there, trying to get it.
It's the way you think you were?
I believe I was in the baby carriage.
The baby carriage.

And I was born in the month of April, and the leaves were darker green must have been May or June, bigger. And I imagine it was a bird up there and I was reaching for this bird. I remember that. Then I remember I had -- all of a sudden, I looked up and there was a brother.
(Laughter.)

And I liked him. He was a nice little fella. I remember praying with him and then I remember that he had -- something was running out of his nose and he made a certain noise when he was breathing and I remember that. So it seems that -- and the next thing I remember is that I didn't see him no more and I found out that he and I were in the hospital with the diphtheria and scarlet fever and he didn't make it and I remember that they gave me a cold liquid and it was milk and I didn't know it then, but when I tasted it, I said (inaudible).

Now, I've got another thing in memory. I was at-- I remember I was at a sink, a washing basin or something, and I was reaching up there to get something and I remember falling and cutting my lip and they give me a medicine and I didn't know what it was then, but later, when I tasted them, I smelled this particular medicine, I knew it was Dobell's solution that they had (inaudible).

Now, as mama -- she was working all the time and I was little, but I had my ideas, too. I was weaving other webs too, you know, and I remember just walking -- I must have been toddling and I remember that my mother was walking with me one time and a lady took me and was kissing me and my mother and myself weren't ________. We're not kissing people. We're not too -- there's a look in the eye and that's it. We know. So as my mother said, (Unintelligible)
give him to me. He has lost what he was born with. And my mother says, "Yes, I know." I was born with that too, and by the way, my mother --
What was she talking about?
Being born with -- complete with -- enveloped with that veil that I had enveloped. She said, "I (inaudible)." "What did it look like?" He said, like a ham.
(Laughter.)

(Inaudible) slapped me three times and all of a sudden, I made it. So I kept all of these things in mind and then I remember various little small things about having my little childish ideas and dreams. I had a hobby horse (inaudible), but I put a (unintelli- gible) on it and I was driving this hobby horse (inaudible). Then I remember -- now I remember we moved from E Street to I Street and there was a little fella whose name was William Watson. I believe his father was Haitian because my mother was speaking a language to him and they were communicating and this man was a very hot-tempered man and he was a very proud man. He had a little restaurant and Willie was the only child and they spoiled Willie. Poor Willie, he -- "I want candy," and they give him candy. So Willie, one time we took a little adventure, we wanted to move out from our little section. So it seemed like we walked say from Virginia Avenue up to Dupont Circle -- that's a long way for two little fellas -- and then it seems as though
Willie got excited and started making a lot of those sounds and making a lot of crying and sounded terriable and I didn't appreciate him. I didn't appreciate that. So --
(Recording interruption.)

And we made so much noise until the police come and took us to the station house and it seems as though Willie wasn't satisfied with crying. He got on the floor and started rolling on the floor and then I jumped on Willie.
(Laughter.)

I said, 'Why are you making this noise?' And so he says, 'Well, ask Willie where he lives.' And Willie didn't know nothing. I says where I live, on 2219 E Street, and I know you catch the F train when you go home and that's where I live and I can get home, if I could get -- let me take him home. So then they went and got my mother and Willie went into his act until they give Willie a whole lot of ice cream. We were never friends after that. I wouldn't take Willie nowhere with me. Willie was one of those type of fellas who want to take you somewhere. So from that day on, no one takes me nowhere. No one.
How old were you then?
I believe I was about three or four, because I hadn't gone to school, see? I hadn't made school and then, now, he's happy too. Doing his act. So now,

then my mother's moved back to E Street, right across from the school, and I started school and learning was something I had to have. I knew I had to have it. I had to have knowledge. I knew that. So I went to kindergarten and kindergarten was nothing for me. I was making rabbits and horses and little--- those blocks. So they took me out of kindergarten and put me in first grade and I was moving beautifully and I'd tie my shoes and fix (inaudible) and be in school on time and everything.

So then this passed on and then later, first and second grades, (inaudible). But my mother was working at a place called Hardicht's Brewery and at that time, there was nobody to take care of me and my brother, so we would -- they had a kindergarten in Hardicht's Brewery (German is) people and they had a school for the help that were working there.
How did they spell their name?
(Unintelligible).
I mean the people who had --
The German..... ?
Yeah.

His name was Chris (PHONETIC) or C-r -- C-h-r -- h-i-r-t-c-h. Chris Hartch 's Brewery. I think the beer still is on the market in Washington, D.C. at the present time. And so in this kindergarten, we were learning German.

Because we were playing in German and when we go to school we'd be in English because in Foggy Bottom, everyone was down there and you had the Potomac Indian down there and you had the -- well, you had Italian, you had the underclass white man, because he was poor, and you had -- see, you have some Arabs down there, too. So all right, going to school and then the kindergarten and then they gave us a little job of pasting the label on the bottles, on the (inaudible), and they used to give us a sandwich called Braunswiger (PHONETIC) and you just got touch of light beer a little and we was happy fellows.

See, when we got out of this kindergarten (inaudible) they had a ice house. This was next to the Harditch's Brewery too, it was. So we would--very dangerous We were around five or six, you know. We had a lot of (inaudible), too. And we used to ----those big boys used to tell us. "Now you go in there." We'd go through the holes that push the ice through the slot and they'd chop it up and get it out. Now, after thought if one of there on us, we would have those big pieces of ice stuck in / froze to death, because it was a whole building of this frosted ice.

So all right, kindergarten and sixth and seventh grade and from there, then my mother was taking two jobs and she used to do laundry for people and my job was -- well, we had to learn how to cook, we had to learn how to sew and the first thing you had to do is go out in the backyard and scrub the roosters, take care of those--then scrub the fences and that

thing and then you clean up the kitchen and that your first job, then later you'd be cooking and I could cook those cakes and things, and then we'd entertain ourselves a lot, washing and cleaning and keeping things clean and then I became so the ladies -- you know, at that time they wore those little stiff shirts, with the ruffles on them and I could do these, I was the champ -- that was my job, pay you for that.

And by the way, Mama, first I didn't understand what Mama was talking to these animals and those animals was listening and acting accordingly. Says now, I don't want you 'round here, because you got them old bugs on you, I want you to stay away from here and here's a bone and I'll give you -- but stay away from here. This dog was scratching and going on and here, the dog -- and the cats, she'd talk to the cats. So I didn't pay it no mind, so I didn't say nothing.

And so around about 8 or 9, I was living on Virginia Avenue and George Washington Circle, (unintelligible) and she sent me to get some clothes to be washed, and on the way there was a dancing place, called it Jordan St. Mark's and I heard -- the first time -- I heard a little bit of piano playing, but I heard the violin and I was enchanted by this. I said, oh, what is that! And then I lingered a little too long and Mama was wondering what happened and why are you so late. so I said, what's that, and she said oh, that's the violin and later on I saw the big bands and I think it was -- the band

was People of Color and later I think it was Ford Dabney's band. They had big _____phones and the people they were beautiful, (unintelligible) and so that was it and my mother and my family, they would sing. Now, these people, they wasn't too strong on education, but they was singing solfeggio--- do-re-mi-fa-so-la-ti-do; they were singing and (unintelligible) so then what--
What kind of songs were they singing.

Some of them they was singing some old French songs, but they had something else, some funny words in there. It sound more like French-African or something like that and (unintelligible) and then they would answer because --
Could you sing one of them?
I can't -- couldn't get nothing because there wasn't no piano. So I listened to that and then when I was round about 10, I'm going fast now and down at the YMCA setting pins, see, setting pins --
Setting pins.
You set them with your hands, now they have machines but before you had to get down and take all these ten pins and --
Was this a white or black bowling alley?
The YMCA.
Did black people come in there.
I don't think they'd be too welcome in there, so --
: Only in -- you could work in there and set --

In the capacity of servitude and they had one boy who was a nice -- I forget what that boy's name was, Fred -- I'll just call his name Fred, he lived on Virginia Avenue, he was studying all the time. He was a great pianist, so by working and setting pins, I knew -- then I became more -- then I heard Meyer Davis' orchestra when the crystal sets come in and then everything opened up to me.
: Now, the war was going on.
No, the war, it hadn't started yet.
: You were born in 1909.
Yeah, born in 1909.
: At 10, it was 1919.
I think we were studying all of the Allies generals and everything in Marseille, but yes, the war -- when you're a little boy -- you know, you --
: You don't remember much about it.

Wait, just a moment, then one of my uncles come up, an uncle he come up. Mama was talking Creole all the time and then there was an Indian-looking man come in there and he was very sick and now, they was talking Indian, so Mama and the man (unintelligible) I didn't know what it was,

and Mama slapped me down. I was staring, and Mama, pop, don't you ever (unintelligible) and the man stayed there and the man beautiful come out/and went on to Chicago (unintelligible) start singing and humming and going on, and I'm right there listening to it.
Wait a minute, she took him in a room.

Took him -- and he didn't come out -- he had to come out to do whatever it was doing, had to be done, probably, but this man stayed there, about three weeks -- I hadn't seen this before and it was awful.
The disease he had.

Now, I think it would have been Parkinson's disease, because he -- he was shaking a little and he couldn't control his saliva and things like that, so Mama, I said -- yeah, I know voodoo, everybody knows voodoo --
Somebody did something to him.

But I let it go, because it wasn't in my realm of thinking. So, all right, I said (unintelligible) and by the way, you see at that time, every young boy at that time had a uniform that he wore. My uniform was a pair of, for Christmas, you get a Norfolk suit of corduroy and you get two pair of stockings, ribbed stockings and they come up to here and then you had a pair of shoes, Buster Brown shoes and had a big toe on them, I hated those big toes and it had a copper on it and laced up and come up -- so then you had to have a cap and then you had long underwear, the underwear was

only covered, went down to -- and you had to learn how to put the underwear in your socks, that big bulge in there and knickers then you did those and you had to get them a certain way, but we found a way and we rolled them so they'd look cute. them a certain way You rolled / so they'd come up real nice, --
: The stockings.

No, the pants over the stockings. So now that was -- you had two shirts and the shirts, you had to keep them clean and you had a tie and you had to know how to fix that. That was your uniform, poor me, about the second week the knees was out of those pants and them shoes. I taken a hammer and beat that big knob off of there and then my nose was always running and always sticking out -- cold and my nose running and I was beautiful. I'd come to school and the thing that was happening, I had problems, I think a lot of problems, then the school, the whole thing was--later on, it was suggested or something was said, oh, Jack, smell like pee-peee, hurt my feelings so bad, then they got (unintelligible), somebody smell like pee pee. Oh, my goodness.

And I said, I don't---- but when I passed 7 or 8 years old, it disappeared, so that was -- during that time, everything I'd do, I do all types of things, and my mother says, that's all right, don't worry about it, so everything was beautiful.
I was about 10 years old, then I starting thinking

about seriously, I like music, but I always wanted to be one of those generals too, you know, oh, yes, I wanted to be -- they moved me, but then there was man, his name was -- my uncle was named Uncle William, he'd come up from New Orleans, then lived in a house called Mr. Dorsey, his family is Indian and he had everything in his family. He come from Annapolis, Maryland. Great contractors now, and Mr. Dorsey, --
What was his name?
Mr. William Dorsey.
Dorsey, D-o-r-s-e-y.

That's right, and Mr. Dorsey liked me and I liked Mr. Dorsey, he was the one who worked on the wagon, called the White Wing, when the horses -- White Wing would get this stuff off the street because in Washington at that time the streets was clean, clean as could be and Mr. Dorsey would come and White Wings, they had white coats on and they looked something -- had something looked like our garbage can now and put this in his wagon and I'd be up there with Mr. Dorsey and that stuff was smelling and it smelt like perfume to me, I was so happy. I was the happiest man up there with Mr. Dorsey.

So now here is my first sadness. He come up in the draft and he had to leave, see, and I had another uncle, he married my aunt, he had to leave, but Mr. Dorsey had to leave but before Mr. Dorsey got his draft notice, I was sleeping -- I don't know if I was sleeping or not, three pigeons come in

the window, I saw, I think I saw and I woke right up and I was -- and I said Mama, three pigeons and she says, yes, I know, son and then the next day there was Mr. Dorsey, there was my foster, not my foster -- but by marriage, he had to go and then there was another person that had to go, so Mama said, (unintelligible) she didn't put too much to it, but she knew, but I didn't know. I didn't know about that.

So, all right, everybody come back and by that time Mama was telling me something else, and I'm looking around talking halfway bassing, see, I done grow too big for Mama so when Mama really wants something happen, Mama would grab me by the arm and drop that tooth on me and bite me so badly, yes, Mama, anything, she'd be chewing on me. Mama was a very small woman, she had very small feet and small -- and whatever Mama wanted done, I did that, and did it quickly, and nothing was no problem.

So it seems like, I was going to school and everything and then I think I was about 13 -- I had a little ukele and was playing it (unintelligible) and there was a man named Emmy Lucas, he worked down through Harditch's Brewery and they sent him to school and he was a genius. He knew all the music, that's what he did and he was a pianist and he told me, he says, study, he was a dogmatic man. Don't come to my house unless you have some music and don't make no bad notes in here, go home, these kind of things, so I worked and I got -- no, what happened,

I was working to get a clarinet and my mother sent me to Louisiana on vacation and I had an accident which changed everything, because I used to be a good swimmer and good runner and I boxed and everything and was doing pretty good, but by the way, when I was about two years, or three years old, I saw my mother and the streetcar was coming up the street and I ran to meet my mother and the streetcar cut the sandal off from my ankle, so, I'll tell you about that later.

And then the same summer that I was going on vacation, in August, to my grandparents, I dived into the wharf where we always swim at and an old piece of rusty tin cut the back of my right leg and it became black, so these warnings were going on. I didn't know it. So I had a very serious accident.

So which left me an amputee so now when I come back to the station, this is one of the worst parts of my life. My mother looked at me, looked me in the eye like this and I looked at her and we didn't say a word for two weeks. It was nothing said, nothing. Here you are son, then we could talk. I understood the pain that she had, because I had accepted that. I said that's it, we must do other things, so then later she said, I knew it -- I knew it was going to happen -- she said, when the streetcar hit that leg, it was then (unintelligible) so we never said a word anymore about that. We started doing what we had to do and now, I'm looking, realized what I was working to do, down at the YMCA, so now, I said I have got to

make it now, and I said my music, but all my little friends, they come by to visit and I have some good friends and I had some devils too, so the devils went and found me a cornet or soprano saxophone, a violin. They found me all those things and that summer before I had been playing with a fellow's crutches and those things I had to use, so all right, now this gets, I said I got to have some type of transportation or mobility in myself, so I went and asked the man for the job setting pins, and I'd hop and sometimes the guys was trying to throw in on me, so I had to --
When you say they tried to throw in on you.

See, how rotten some people are sometimes. You set one, two, three, four,five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, but each guy throwing and I guess he wanted to see me hop to get out of the way of the pins and so I -- those duck pins would fly and sometime the pin would fly all the way up and I'd hop up, and this had to be done, and I did it and so -- I don't think I needed that amputation (unintelligible) too sad --
We're going to get a whole lot of stuff, that's just going to be part of it.
Well, I worked and bought -- went to a -- bought a leg, an artificial leg and all the colors, I can't understand what happened, the man give me a cherry red limb

to put on my body and I am a brown-skinned man and I can't understand that but I used a cane about a couple of weeks and after that I forgot about the cane and that was it. Then I began to study the clarinet. I studied the clarinet and there were five buddies I had, they were called the Walker family. They too were from Georgia and Louisiana and -- Indian people and Negro people mixed.
Well, all of them they bought saxophones, the two brothers bought saxophones and one other bought a trumpet, so I got an idea, I'm going to create, I'm going to make a band.
How old were you then?

13, 14, 15. I said I'm going to make this band and I was coming into high school too, so I studied the clarinet and the band what it seems those -- this boy's name, Phineas, Phineas was on the trumpet but he just wasn't playing that music and he was my best friend. I got that old cornet that I had and got -- looked at the chart and got down and started playing.

Now, we had -- in this band, we had -- at one point Albert Heights, a violinist, we had a pianist, beautiful pianist, he come from the southwest part of Washington, then we had a full band and by the way, we had a boy named Daniel Braseers(?) which later he became one of the greatest jazz trumpets that is known. They used to call him Georgetown, and he was in the band. So we were rehearsing and across the street, the man had

to eat a bulldog, he was bad, he wanted / everybody up, but when we were rehearsing, the bulldog, he'd walk in and get right under what's this boy's name, Phineas' feet and stay there. He must have loved what Phineas wasn't playing, because Phineas wasn't playing nothing. And Mama had to whisper, "that/ dumb dog," (unintelligible) Mama said, well, you stay there now and don't let nobody else come in. People coming in the windows and everything, so the dog took care of his business and then people baking cakes and all the people around us was happy about it and stuff lemondae and ham / so everybody come to rehearsal.

All right. We did this say about six months, then I'm feeling good now, so I was going to school and then I was -- there was a boy named Arthur Lanier on the clarinet. I liked the clarinet and I was still studying the clarinet but I was playing the second part on the trumpet, so then I found that the clarinet didn't have the melody and so I said, I'd better change over to the trumpet and -- for the second instrument. So I begin to play the trumpet and by having the sense of Training melody, I was playing in the Manual / School Orchestra and I played a solo and I got the valedictorian and I was playing the melody, it was (humming) The sonority was pure.
Can you sing it?
"Ave Maria". But it's hard to play and and become valedictorian it's hard to sing and I got breath control/and then there was a fellow there by the name of Rudolph Eglin, this boy was a
well, he loved life, so I got in his band and --
What does he play.

He plays everything. He plays soprano sax and he played piano and could arrange, now during this time Duke he was in Deanwood, see, now the big bands, Claude Hopkins, he was a big band, and then they had a band called Sam Taylor's and Sam Taylor would give you a little trouble and they had one called Cyrus Carter's Jazzhounds. Those days they had -- they all had names, just awful names. Blues Stompers, Barefoot Ramblers and one band was named Sam somebody and his Yarddogs.

So now Sam Taylor, he was -- you don't go in Southwest and bother Sam Taylor, he'd get you and this -- and Cyrus Carter, he'd get you if you go in Northwest, so that was -- and then they had the White Brothers, they were society. You didn't bother with me, and they all read music. Cyrus Carter wasn't studying about no music, and was swinging and going on --
What kind of tunes did they play?

They had one called 'Senorita Mine.' (Humming) and they tore that 'Senorita' up and swung it to death. 'Blind Man' And (humming) I think the _____Blues' and you can't get a monkey go get yourself a shimmyback, down at Shimmy Hall.' So and these cats, and I was going and listening to them, so there was a fellow there named Henry Goodman, oh, my goodness, he'd hit high C, and that was the first time I ever heard -- Henry Goodman -- he had his style and he was popping those notes, so
I hadn't heard Louis Armstrong yet, so then I go to the theatre I kept listenting to that clarinet there and it was moving me, but I couldn't get away from that trumpet.
(Side B)
I stayed with Rudolph Eglin.
How do you spell his name.
E-g-l-i-n.
So I got what I need from Rudolph, I was playing polinaises and then there was a --
Were these Negro or white places.

These were Negro places, see, Washington, D. C. what you didn't have, if you had that money that white man's next to you, see, you living there and I couldn't understand there was no scuffling about the schools in the section. because you didn't think about it, and this fellow was going to school, to some other school and they used to have those competitive drills and things and home boy would put down so much stuff out there on the field of honor, so --
You mean you had these competitive drills with whites.
First, you'd see, there were two high schools, Dunbar High School and Armstrong Manual Training, and they had the uniforms you know, ROTC.
And they was colonels, and captains, and things and those cats were marding and things and they were taking care

of business, then at the end of the season they all quit doing, they'd all come out on the field and march and then one who won, he challenged the boys in gray and oh, my goodness, one guy had orders, so he was running up to the band all of a sudden, then he ran and did something in that arms and them spread all out and he won the cup, won it every year, so people get imagination, so now coming back to this music, that was a band.

Now, the White Brothers they were a society band. Zeke ? was playing in that band, Harry White and there were four brothers, Harold White, Edward White, Sparky White, about four, and Zeke was in there, now all those boys, you see, you had to watch Washington during that time. Washington had what they called "high yellow" people and see, that society now, these people had all them good big jobs, man, and they owned all their homes and they was up there, so when these other people -- well, anyway, Harry White -- I mean White Brothers played for the Smart Set.

And when the White Brothers couldn't play for the smart set, well, the Bluebirds would come in and I joined the Bluebirds, and we played that pretty music too, and everybody was up there, looking pretty and and then everybody was kind of halfway yellow in there, see, but the thing when they're getting them dances, they'd have something over the door, I imagine there was something over that door, and if you didn't fit that thing, you wasn't getting in there. Or do you belong

to the club, well, no, I'm so sorry, but we can't allow you to come in but they had right next door the Pythian Hall, you may go in there. Oh, swell over there, and that's all them doctors and lawyers and things, see, so we up there playing there and them waltzes and all that beautiful stuff.
Do you remember what some of the favorite tunes were.

Well, sure, (singing) 'I wonder what become of Sally.' Well, they were copying from Meyer Davis, anytime some new piece would come out, they would play it. Five Foot Two, Eyes of Blue and they'd get that music and shade it and we had that together.
When you say you'd get it shaded, what do you mean.

You read the dynamics, see, you read the dynamics. You didn't know you had to do it, then you'd bring it down and you'd read that and it makes all the sound beautiful, especially when we're playing waltzes and the one waltz we played was the Champagne Waltz. (Humming) Something like Lawrence Welk is doing, like that, and those women with that high class perfume and looking good and that's it.

So, all right, I stayed with them a long time till I got -- but what was happening to me, I was having -- my last year of high school, I was having a big problem, see, trying to make those gigs and try to study, and study those books, the

mathematical was about eating me up, but those people they was going to the dances and so on, I passed, but when I got to the sophomore year in college, it was rough, rough, rough and I barely made it, I just barely made it, but then I'm getting more worldly with the instrument.
Where did you go.

Howard University, because see at that time Duke had left there. Claude Hopkins' family, I think they was -- his mother or something was a professor or somebody dean or something, see, Claude Hopkins was a very high class individual. He's a dogmatic man, but in his way, he's all right. He's beautiful. That's the real Washingtonian way and by the way, Sonny Greer will tell you about those Washingtonian, and then I went to the theatre, the Howard Theatre one time and I looked at the show, it was called Shake Your Feet Revue, and I saw the trumpet player. I said well, I should be down there and leave here. See, I want to leave now. So I went down there and met a fellow named Sylvester Lewis, and he said, yes, we need a second trumpet, so I got out there and I read the music pretty good and there was another friend of mine named Herbie Cowans, boy from Texas. He said, by the way, how old are you. I was about 16 then, and he said you get out of here, man, they'd put him in jail. If I was in that pit and they caught me in there, they'd put me in jail -- I mean wouldn't put me in jail, (Inaudible) so I

had to forget that. So now I'm playing my gigs and things are running smooth. So they had a little gathering up on the second floor, called the Smart Set Social Club, so I said I'm going up here and try my hand out in the gambling. I went up there and they paid me $5.00 for that gig and I said, there wasn't nobody up there but the caretaker,whatever he was and this man had hands about 10 inches long and the stick was almost that long. He said, all right, then, here we go. I said $1.00. I threw them dice on 12, so I was ready to ride. On 2, 2 again, 12, then 2. I said that's life, that's the way you do it.
So when I got to the stairs that man put his foot all of the way up in my derriere and I come all the way down those stairs. He said if you ever come in again, I will -- you know.

Now, from U Street, from 11th and U to 22nd and E, first you got to go all the way to 11th, you got 11 blocks to go, long blocks, Washington blocks to go and then you got to come down from U to E Street, so I made that -- I never had any desire to try to gamble, never, so I'm happy about that. I am extremely happy.

So all right, then I was at a little dumpy theatre, it's called the Mid-City Theatre, and they had a jazz band in there and they had a fellow named King Swayzee; he come from Arkansas and he looked like one of them -- not Cherokee, like a Pawnee Indian, so King Swayzee, he was in this show and he had a fellow named Eichelberg on the saxophone, had a guy on trombone,
and I said I would like to join this band They needed a second trumpet and said get right in there.
So I was so excited that I just left, just cut out. So then I wrote my mother when I was on the road, went on down to [St.] (Virginia) Petersburg and I was so happy. The man wasn't paying me nothing.

Oh, you know, it's awful the theatre manager, owe for the drops, and I wasn't getting nothing, just enough to eat with, but I was happy, but I was so happy, man, so then we played all that summer. I wrote my mother (unintelligible) and she said what about school and I barely made it, so I just dropped out, just disappeared and then -- but I had gotten that bug and then I was saying, then I heard this Ike Dixon and Ford Dabney then Fletcher Henderson come down and shook everybody up and at that time, now, Duke had just come to New York, so I said my goodness, then Claude Hopkins went to Europe in 1923, see. I think it was Spain or somewhere and Henry Goodman left and when Henry didn't come back, he was telling me (unintelligible)
What was he talking about.

He was telling me (unintelligible) so I said I'll keep that in mind, so now this was called Sammy Lewis Bamboo Follies, so and this King Swayzee, he said he so he didn't sound like Louie, he sound like King Oliver and all the fellows who had heard King Oliver, like Lips Page and Louis Metcalfe, well, they said King Oliver was the/thing and I asked Louis one time, was he really that good, and he said I am only a bandaid on his rib, he said that man was something

else. He said the man could play concert trumpet, he could play everything, everything he could do. He knows just when not to make a whole lot of notes, he know when to make a whole lot of notes, and he said and I was playing second trumpet with him and he fired me, and I cried. He run me out of the band for me to take a job across the street, that's what he told me.
So this band, we did all this summer and we got stranded in Newark, New Jersey and they got some money and we went back to Washington. We gigged around there quite a few times, or Baltimore.
What was Newark like - Newark, New Jersey like

I was about 17 then. Newark, New Jersey, there weren't many people of color there. Most of them Indian people, mixed Indian people and German people. And naturally they had the white man and that's what was happening. And so I got stranded and then I went home. Then I went back with the Bluebirds and I stayed and saved myself up about a couple hundred dollars and got a couple of nice suits and then I said, but I'm going, so I come right back to Newark, New Jersey, but I had met a little girl up there and I went and knocked on the door and it seemed like the biggest police dog come out there smoking, so I abandoned the idea of that romance.
So I messed around Newark, New Jersey until I kept studying with a man named Emory Lucas, music.

he says, well, Jack, why don't you go up to the Big Apple and see a man named Professor Jackson, so I says okay, and I went up there and Professor Jackson, couldn't hardly hold the clarinet and so they had another fellow named Joe Crump and Joe Crump had a whole set of gold teeth and had diamonds on each side and this little funny looking place, so he says well, can you play anything so I played the melody and he said, that's nice, so he said can you come to work, and so Jackson said yes, so then come to work tonight and then Jackson disappeared.

Now, that night people, we're playing and it seemed like people started arguing out in the street on the other side of town and they come up there and fight it out and cut it up, so see, Joe couldn't read so I said Joe, now that's F, what do you mean, oh, yes, and right across the street Joe had his bordello right across the street -- well, I won't give you the name of the street -- it was something there --
A whorehouse.

Yes, something like that and his girl-friends were snatching people so I didn't -- I wanted to know what was happening and Joe was saying now, now, you -- he used to call me Him all the time, so -- I was getting myself together you know, I was learning - and one chick come in there and I'm looking too and he says get away from this bandstand because she had made it possible for another fellow to have died by
request, so she said, after all, I can look and he's nice -- get away from here, and Joe got up and put a little flesh upside that child's head and she didn't come near that bandstand anymore.
So now me and Joe, I'm teaching Joe and he's teaching me that stuff.
Where had you learned the harmony and stuff.
I'm still learning -- I learned in Washington, but he moved to Newark, New Jersey. I studied there, I had gotten my book.
You were into advanced harmony.

Classic harmony and then I mess with the counterpoint, but I had no place to use it and in fact, recognize what I heard, so I stayed up there and one day they said, have you heard. They said, what happened, Joe was found in bed with the singer, and the husband come in and hit Joe in the head with some iron pipes. I said, what. So that night come on the job with some vaseline on his head. There's a little abrasion so he said let's play, let's go, everything was all right.

Now, I lived way upstairs, there wasn't nobody in the hotel but me living. I couldn't understand that, but I was up there and I was sleeping, feeling good and the chef was kind of weird and he had them pretty women too and the boss

was named Stony, he was an Israeli man, so one night I had gone upstairs and gone to bed, and right next to the Big Apple was a synagogue and Willie the Lion, well, Willie the Lion and his brother, they were going to that synagogue, because Willie the Lion is a Catholic. His brother Melvin, the whole family, so now --
Did you meet him there.

No, I met his brother, but he knew of me, Willie the Lion was a big man in New York. I hadn't made New York yet. I was over there. So while I was sleeping it seems as though that the man who owned the place had enraged the chef and the chef creased his head with a cleaver, so wasn't nobody in -- the doors were locked, but I could get out the back, you know, and I was in there by myself, and the chef had left was what necessary to be eaten and I stayed there about three months, and then I said, well, my goodness, I can't stay up here all the time. Grove Street was terrible, it was an awful street, but I knew everybody and Joe was back in there resting himself, playing cards and he said, don't worry about it. We got everything we need, but I found, I would have had to get into that circuit. So one day I went to the Orpheum Theatre and I'm lucky. That day the trumpet player got sick and didn't make it and I ran home and got my horn and got in that pit and they were playing all the numbers in the chorus, the chorus was playing all the numbers, that I mostly knew and I didn't have no not too many heavy strong pit music, and they didn't

let me play for the motion pictures, because had I played for the motion pictures, they would have got me. So I got in that pit and set that pit afire, got the job immediately so that was all right, and then I really started then (unintelligible) his name was Joe James, he's got a son, named Joe James also, he's a big man, so Joe taught me everything, trumpet, and they had a man named Clarence Adams, one of the greatest clarinets I've ever heard. He was from Winston-Salem, North Carolina and this I realized he said you look like a man I know and I said yeah, who, and he says John Adams. Plays trombone and he also plays mandolin and he owns a barber shop and he owns the busline and I said, yes, that's what he is.
Did you encounter this cat named Seminole at that time.
Yes, indeed!
/Seminole was in Sammy Lewis' band with the Bamboo Follies. Yes, Seminole, this man was left-handed and it sounded like two pianos, that he was playing and the same thing with the banjo and guitar.

Yes, Seminole -- people coming from out in Maryland, some of them hillbillies of color and Banjo Bernie, there's one of them, why these people--and Snowden;ible) so all right, I stayed in that pit, I stayed in that pit a long, long time and then a circus -- no, it was Johnny Jones 101 Ranch comes to town and a boy, first time I ever seen a

I'm turning 18.

Oh, yes, because we had to play the music for the silent moving pictures. We had a -- we played all that music and it was called William Tell's 'Overture' and great they had a violinist; his name was Floyd Hickman. But all these people were masters,
These were all Negroes.

These were virtuosos: a boy named Ted Nixon, trombone. They had a bass man, played cello and all these things. You get up there and do your act, and he'd write

it out for you, and so -- and I was getting all that heavy music and that give me experience and now-- so the 101 Ranch came to New Jersey, Newark, and I became a friend with Eddie Durham and all his brothers, we became very staunch friends.

And well, I know 101 Ranch closed and me and Eddie Durham was all tight, we hit it off together, we were a team, and we used to play our gigs together and get our little riffs together and then we started creeping over to New York. At that time the dancing schools were in vogue, so we're going to dancing school and set the dancing school on fire, we would get a job.

But then they started saying we can't have no trombone, got to use the trumpet (unintelligible) so we used that particular pattern for quite some time and then Eddie, I think he left and went west and then I come to New York and now the first place I went was to New York, I went to Small's Paradise and Teddy Hill, I think was playing the saxophone. A fellow named June Clark, a great trumpet player. I think you might remember him as being Ray Robinson's second. He and Sonny Greer grew up together. Their fathers owned race horses and I think it was Asbury Park or somewhere down there --
Long Branch.

Right down there, so here I am, at that time I didn't -- I was there and so yes, son, what do you want. I had my little bag and it was hot and I had a big woolen suit on and the suit looked good, so -- yes, son, what do you want now.

I say, 'I want to come in.' (Unintelligible)/ Yeah, how old are you? 18, sir. Now, wait now, and then Teddy Hill saw me and he said come on in here, man and (unintelligible) June Clark said yes, and I sit down and that waiter come over wiping the table, see those waiters can wipe those tables, you know, watching you. What kind of Coca Cola you want.

I said, Coca Cola so now -- Myra Johnson, bless her, she's my little buddy. She saw that man was getting ready to get me so she says, 'Come here, little fellow.' I say yes. She says 'Are you geechy?' and I said 'Yes, I'm geechy,' because people from New Orleans and South Carolina, they call each other geechys, so especially when you speak that patois, so now --
You speak it.

Yeah, I -------and it come in very, very handy because when I first went to France, well, I could make myself understood, so now, here's what happened she says, well, give him a Coca Cola, well, yeah, all right, she says where you living at, and this is about 10 o'clock at night and I said I have no place and she went -- not to him whispered to but somebody up there and June Clark and the rest of the fellows so what happened is they said yes, and she said, are you tired and (unintelligible) she said, well, you go upstairs and took me upstairs and put me on the front room way up top there and the place was clean and beautiful towels and beds

were nice and clean but there was nobody up there but me so I stayed up there two weeks and I got frightened and I didn't know what that house was doing. They were snatching people up what it's for; and taking care of business and that's so I stayed two weeks and I left, then I went down on 32nd Street and asked the lady for a room, but I smelled the very pungent odor and that odor it was too much, incense and I think it was opium that I was smelling, and she looked like she had this makeup on, yes, young man, I said (unintelligible) so I cut out.

So I started living on Edgecombe Avenue) and I was living right across the street from one of my aunts and didn't know it. She didn't know it either, so now I'm here in this big city as you said, and I'm seeing lights and guys are going through the Tree of Hope and I'm meeting these big stars. I was going to a place called the Rhythm Club, Jelly Roll Morton, Fletcher Henderson, Coleman Hawkins, and Elmer Williams, and Rex Stewart -- by the way, he's from Washington and I'm meeting these and Ovie Alston and Sandy Williams, these people. I even seen Henry Goodman, I haven't seen these people. These people at this time they're wearing tight pants and velvet coats and Metcalfe had a Cadillac and -- Bojangles and all these stars, and these pretty ladies, oh, my goodness. I was really in wonderland, so then all right, (unintelligible) so Jelly Roll Morton says look, what you doing around here. I said, sir, I would like to have a job and he said, do you

read music. Yes, sir. Where you come from anyway (unintelligible) no, sir, I come from Lafayette, Louisiana. Can you read music. Yes, sir, well, go and get it. This is 12 o'clock in the day. I got my tuxedo and put it on. Read that. I read it.
Where were you?
At the Rhythm Club in front of everybody. Read that. So I read it. He said, go home and take your tuxedo off and then come back at 8 o'clock here. Yes, sir.

I did it and so Jelly Roll and some man there was named Al somebody, wearing a big diamond ring, and Jelly Roll opened up, cursing the chick out, come up here you so and so: and sing a song, and don't you rush the tempo and you hear what I said, and she was crying. Get up there now and he started playing one of them gut bucket things--take that mute and put it in that half pocket and I did just that. I stayed there and Jelly Roll Morton and he was -- those poor women, was in awful shape and the gangsters come in, Jelly --he'd sing "Mr. Jellord," he was taking that stuff bad and come on round there -- was really getting straight.

So then it seemed like overnight, seeing that thing happen like it happen -- something happen and wouldn't nobody come to work. Can't go over there now, little later, little later, then we went to work and some guys come in there and Jelly Roll Morton say come on, let's get behind the piano and then make it out the back door and that's what we did and then

Jelly Roll Morton get out there and preach about the valuation of Negro man and the white man, dogs and roaches and things being equals and he would say, it was awful. A human / to dead police dogs in the backyard, so he would --
He would say what.
(Unintelligent conversation)
No morals, he was terrible.
How could he --

His name was Ferdinand Alexander Morton, so he was a stickler for morals and yet he was running all the bordellos. But that's the way he was. And so I just listened to him and I said, I ain't none of them kind of people, "Mr. Jelly Roll, and he said, "I wasn't talking to you. I'm talking about them people out there." (Unintelligible)
So then now I went to dancing school, I'd go into a dancing school and you know, at that time when you're young and them chicks is looking and you're looking too, so we was working --
Is this still Morton's band.
No. I was only playing -- Morton and I was only playing together. I wasn't -- wasn't anybody playing -- on drums, he had his feet doing that drum work and he always played -- had the bass there.
When you were dealing with him, did you find that he -- how was his harmonic knowledge.
When he played, he knew. (Unintelligible) he was the person who put it on paper. He was the first one to put it on paper.
Now was he using a -- what about -- do you know what -- was he playing any like whole-tone scales.

No, they were just simple scales. Pass it on the scales. He didn't move no further than that seventh or ninth, then he'd go into the diminish every now and then, but he'd just say right on that, that first -- fourth, fifth, of course, he might make a sixth come down, but you could understand anything he was doing, but he would do so much (unintelligible) and so then now I went -- then I got a job -- I'm a man, I'm getting a mustache and getting side-burns and things, so I got a job working with another man from Washington, D. C. His name is Cliff Jackson, so I'm coming conscious because everybody studying harmony, from a man named Mr. Hall, everybody studying and a boy named Horace Knight was up there. Another man, aged man, his name is Aaron and Cliff is on the piano and a man named Hank Larson on the drum, very beautiful drummer.

So you read and we're getting all these heads and when your music started to change, had a thing called the "Louisiana Bobo," it had syncopation and Archie Bleyer was writing a lot of things that had syncopation, lot of syncopation and that's the first time we seen -- and it was a school for me.
Do you remember the way any of those pieces went?

Like (humming) that was the Louisiana Bleyer Bobo. And Archie had a thing called Saturday Night something, but it was all (humming) crazy rhythm and some other stuff, but at that time rhythm was going on, see (humming) 'Putting on the Ritz,' all this is going in these shows. This is when Gershwin was writing all this beautiful music.
Was he coming down to the club to see the guys.

He was going -- he was studying with knew up on St. Nicholas Avenue an old man from New Orleans that I / and this old man said that he gave someone his score of 'Afrikana' and I heard that -- I heard what he had in that score of 'Afrikana' and it sounded like a tune that I hear.
Of Gershwin's.
Of tunes that I hear around. So that's what the man told me. Now, --
Who was this guy that Gershwin studied with.

This old Dave Faulk, or something like that and he told me, this man -- I would come down by there every night and this master -- see, there's a certain thing musicians about masters that you hear strains coming up you listen.
He was playing keyboard .

Yes, and you could hear all these master things and this classic stuff and you -- listen, I knocked on that door. I wanted to know and this big man come in there and the dog wanted to take me out and he told the dog, no, and we became friends, and he told me (unintelligible) but I made a mistake (unintelligible)

For example, Art Tatum was playing all that stuff but it doesn't sound like he's playing, he don't put no tag to what he's doing so this is what I'm saying.
Now, this guy, Gershwin was a student of his.
Yes. I think he went to a German school of Hindemith, because you go to school for certain things and I don't believe that orchestration, for the Rhapsody
in Blue, that Rhapsody in Blue is of an old Hungarian thing.
So you know, that is --
I don't know too much about schooling up here.

them, with Will Vodery,

ful. That was his way. But he knew the horn.

Then I got a job working with this man, Cliff Jackson, as I told you, playing trumpet at a place called the Lenox Club. Johnson.
So, the Cotton Club didn't allow --
Had you seen him many times before that?

I seen him, because he lived up the street from me. I seen him many times. And he was talking so about boxing. And one man asked him, well, what do you think? He said, 'Don't let nobody get to your head, son. Use your head, don't let nobody use it for you.'
(Laughter.)

And he had one of those heads on him. So I got a job up there. And all the stars would come up there, all the people who had money. The number runners, people who owned houses and were making this big money, they would come up there and spoil it.

using all the techniques I had learned on the horn and I was trying to read, because as I told you that new music, that new stuff we come up with, synchopation, and he had a hard one. And another thing was called "Minnie the Moocher" and all these things we were playing --

We come in in the springtime, around March, April, May. It's a beautiful time in Paris. Everybody got to their apartments. Now we're in Paris. Now at that time Paris was the capital of Europe -- the hub for entertainment. In fact, anybody who was anybody even come to Paris, and the money was good. If the money was bad or not, it was beautiful there in France. People like Eddie South, the black angel, he would be coming in from Hungary and you have a fellow named Benny Payton, he's coming in from India..
What did he play?
Benny Payton played the drums. He had a band. He always stayed around in Germany, mostly Austria -- Benny Payton, I think he was from Chicago. Then you had --
How did you like his drumming.
Well, he had been over there a long time. He had been over there a long time and he was a band leader and he know what to do with the people, of course.

He was playing dance music and he was playing music, see, for those people to understand, you must be careful because the people at the time they weren't that jazz conscious -- I mean, they were jazz conscious but you had to make them understand what you were doing.

But he made them understand because when you go way (up in min ill the le) mountains in Switzerland where they speak the Swiss or Dutch they don't want to hear nothing but the St. Louis Blues and then you must sing them a couple spirituals before they're happy. And it's still like that. It's real here in America. You don't have to go nowhere else. It's right here in America, they want to hear those spirituals. Because that's what America is known for.

So you be playing those flatted Fifths and all that stuff, he said we can do that better. (unintelligible) so you just go ahead and play what is you, so so far as his drumming the people liked it, and he worked all the time.

Now, then you had Bricktops, she had her cabaret and you had the Cubans, they were there. Everybody was there. I lived in a hotel called Hotel Rocheschour; it was on Boulevard . Now, Cubans was doing it -- after Afro Cubans stuff and you better be careful, because they'll get you, because you had to play your stuff and play well -- in a big casino, they have a Cuban playing the tipic music and you play jazz, and he'd leave it awful warm out there for you.
When you started putting yourself on there, it started raining and he's happy. Wasn't no sense in moving nothing but jealousy. It was each man doing his stuff and doing it well.

So we had one place called the Cafe Cubane, that's where the Cubans were and right on the hotel where I lived, on the first floor, they had a Russian troupe. They would shake that place up; and right on the corner, where the --
What did the Russians do?

They were singing and singing Russian music. Some of their stuff is still in my head because lots of times when I write music with that piano I hear that stuff. (Unintelligible) and on the corner was the circus.
What was it about the melodies that attracted you to them?

Well, they would play czardas and they were zinganya Russian music, which leans as to gypsy music and if you ever hear a zinganya band, you will know what I'm talking about, you will know exactly what I am talking about.
(Unintelligible)
It was a thing called Shadda (humming) and we'd go on with that beauty and then put it in tempo and that was it and I enjoyed it.
Now, then, on the corner they had a circus. Now, see the circus is not big like big tents and things. It's a

building and seats about I'd say 2,000 people, but those are old circuses. It's a family and they got the building and then across the street, there was a place for the Caribbean people or the Antilles (phonetic) they had a place where they played the bequine and all down that strip that was there, they had a place called Ceile which means heaven and a place called L'Inferno which means hell. They had all these things and the Moulin Rouge was on that strip.

There was entertainment everywhere and now Pigalle, you had and Bricktop had a place in Pigalle, and Mabel Mercer was singing there. That's the last time I saw her. She was singing that beautiful stuff and another place called Melody's Bar. You had a jazz band in there and you had a man named Opal Cooper. Well, Opal Cooper could outsing Caruso. After he lost all his money, he was out singing.
Where was he from?

Opal Cooper, I think he was from Chicago. Then you had Glover Compton and all these fellows -- they had them from all around. They had a bunch of fellows who come out from Spain. They had their Spanish women but a boy named Chase, he come from Washington and one man named Mufflejaws Mars, he come from Washington, D. C. and sure, they was there too, and we would all meet Arthur Laniers also, then you had one fellow who was a jazz violin player named Juice Wilson. He was a violin player, I mean

he was a champ. He stayed in Algeria but he stayed too long. He lost all his finger on the fiddle but he played saxophone. He was something special. See, what happened, the guy had stayed -- he went over there as a young man with a show or something, and he stayed and then he didn't care about keeping up on his instrument. He became of the country where he lived and then you had Englishmen coming over --
You see, Mabel Mercer, I keep talking about her, because she had that most beautiful sound singing and you had the Kentucky singers and you had a man calles Strut Payne.
What did the Kentucky singers do?
Kentucky singers, they sang spirituals and Negro songs. They called them Negro songs and everything and they would set you on fire.
How many of them were there?
Four of them. They would set you on fire. Don't care where they went, they -- when they got finished, it could be raining out there.
Did they use instruments or do it a capello?

They just start out with nothing. No nothing, just start out. Anything in their head. Now, this was the Hot Club of France was there. Now, we had the gypsy band in there playing while we rested. Django was in the gypsy band. Now, Django was playing all that stuff when he

would come to work, and he would come to work, he would have about seven cousins or relatives, or something, they'd all be there and then, one night, you don't see nobody there. Then one night you would see Tango in there by himself and the French fellow who played the bass was called Vola.

Now, when we would get finished, we'd have jam sessions. And there was a fellow named Ainkion (phonetic), very handsome fellow. He was a Czechoslovakian. He could play a lot of saxaphone. He could play a lot of saxaphone and he had another boy named Alex Campbell. He could play a lot of tenor saxophone.
Ainkion, he had heard Benny Carter but he was playing his own style and then we had a fellow who had been over there a long time, a trumpet player and he used to play a lot of trumpet.
Then we had a trombone --
What was his name?
Charlie. I know his name was Charlie but that's all I can remember.
Where was he from? Do you know where he was from?
I don't know. Charlie died. Then you had a, well, Bill Coleman was there and myself and there was another boy named Oscar. Oscar Edmund. He was from the Argentine..
Now, he was playing more guitar than Mango -- Elliot, excuse me. Yes, he could play more guitar.
What was he, Indian or --
Well, he was a man of color. He was a man of color. In fact, we didn't --
His name was what?
Oscar Ellman.
Oscar Ellman?
Yeah, that's right.
E-l-l-m-a-n.
It may be A -- the pronounciation.

Now, all these cats used to be jamming. When I would get finished I would go to the cabaret and stay there and play and play and play. Coleman used to do the same thing. All these dudes did the same thing and then, the King George, "take the mute out, well, he loved jazz. He'd say, let me hear it." He was a big man, big man. Handsome man. This was that, it was beautiful, beautiful.

Now, there were a lot of, in the meantime, people coming there with knickerbockers on, pants, you know, Germans They were coming in and visiting in my hotel. The man was named Josef. He was the clerk and he was the man who would take care of everything. Josef used to speak in German and all this stuff. I didn't pay it no mind.
Then there was quite a few Englishmen, they

After the Germans come out of the Rhineland, everything seemed to be all right. Everybody was calm. There were rumors, he is going to start a war.
Now, we are coming down to 1938, 1938 and I said, I believe I'll go home and see my people, so I went. I come to New York.

in there. That was it. But it wasn't a thing of battering each other, they just played and laughed and drink cognac and go home.

Oh, yes, sure I knew him well. Sure. Because I used to go down there and jam too. Big Boy, I think he had the band and Big Boy was in the band, and that's --

Big Boy played the clarinet, tenor saxaphone and trumpet. He was a born jazzman. You see, you got to watch those people --
Big Boy was --
He was from New Orleans. He was from New Orleans.

Frank -- Francis Goody Goudie. G-o-u-d-i-e, yeah Big Boy, very lovely person, very lovely person.
So, Big Boy, and they worked together. This saxaphone player that I will tell you about later, Robert

MaVumzie (phonetic). MaVumzie was another Charlie Parker, see. He could just hear the notes and he would put them on you, too. He would put them right on you. And he wouldn't be ashamed. You see, we won the prize of France two times but, he didn't take care of his business.

He was from Guadeloupe). That is a sister island of Martinique.

Oh, yes, just like you and I.In fact, we have the same ways, same everything.

Oh, yes, I liked him because he played in my band. I liked him very much. In fact, they thought that I was -- I always got hung up with them -- and when I brought that Cadillac over there, one of them said come on, get in the car -- naw, I ain't gonna get in it. I said, come on -- I thought you was from Guadalupe and you from America. And that's what happened.
Go ahead.
No -- that's a thing that happens you know.

When I left they were coming out from under

Ebony Club. Who owned that?
Well, it was I think, when it started off with a boy named Al Martin.
Al Martin?

Yeah, a fellow named Al Martin. They had gotten this thing down right on Broadway, The Ebony Club. So, I looked at everybody, and at that time, because I had to go back to work, I had about a month or something like that as part of my contract so, I visit everybody, saw everybody and then at that time, Willie Manning says, Jacques, Duke wants to see you, he wants you to get in his band.
I says well, I'm sorry, Willie because I got a contract to go back to Europe and I won't be able to make this one.
Willie Manning went and told Duke that I don't want to be bothered with him. So, now, I can hear what happened. I can hear why that man, every time he saw me
he would be in ice water.

So, I began to hang out with a friend of mine who was a dancer, he was called Freddie and Freddie, he had come in from Europe, Freddie and Al Martin, we would talk And Al Monroe. They were making it. and then Billie Holiday come on the scene/ Billie Holiday began singing beautiful. So, I won't forget this. We, they were going somewhere downtown and the Woodside Hotel it was jumping, it was jumping.
Right next to it was an Italian man named Tony and they had a bar and music in the back.
Now, what street was the Woodside Hotel?
7th Avenue and 141st Street. So, I said they were going down there, down town and I said well, let me off here because I want to play a little bit.
Billie said, yes, let him off here and let him play his little horn. I said that is right, darlin', that is what I wants to do.
And they would give me a couple, a little of that stuff you know and I was right, man. I was right. So, I went in there now, who was playing? I think Sweets was playing.
I says Man, get off of that bandstand and he let me on there and I played.

I got up there and I wailed, and he says, well, you told me to get up and I had to get up there. I said, man, did I do that and he said yeah, you did, you did that. And we laugh about it all the time.

So, all right, after I had taken care of all of my business I went back. But now, this is in the summertime, I went back. And when I got back, the war was in -- so, I said, well, I'll go to Sweden, I can make my way around Europe now.
So now, all right, I was supposed to go back with Willie Lewis and we was supposed to go to Knokke.
All right, but it seems that at rehearsal that Burns insulted me or something and I got up and left. I got up and left and got a job with a Cuban band, Ricco's Creole Band.
Ricco's Creole Band?

Creole band. He played the flute so we went up to Norway and then we would play that stuff now the Norwegans were not aware of jazz, they were aware of it faintly and every night I got off, there was a few fellows up there, they could, they was trying to play so they created a little jazz club and I played and it seems that later they would come in and say I would like to play a few jazz numbers slow.
So, I did this and I became very liked in
Norway and everybody was happy too. We had one boy played the trombone named John degrass. (phonetic)

John, he played the trombone. John could snatch more women. John culd snatch more women in the a street called Radhust Gaten hotel -- we was living in/ (inaudible) and John opened the door and the chick, he snatch her and close the door and then, about an hour later, because those people are very punctual, they come on time. Well, about an hour or hour and a half later, wham, John had snatched one.
I said, John, I don't know what -- there's something, you don't know what they do, but every time he is, whatever they do, they got a chick.
Walter Johnson was one of them kind. He would be playing his drums and chewing chewing gum and at the end, come on, baby, and he's gone. And I didn't know what them people was doing.

John, degrass he was playing the trombone and I never knew what he was snatching, so, but -- and the Cubans, they --they were trying to be noble. was fighting over one of them So I said, why don't you just try to get one of your own and not try to take his? And he said, "You aint no Cuban. Why don't you leave them alone!" So, we stayed up there until summer, we come around August. Around July.
July '39?
Yeah, July '39. I got back, things looked bad. We didn't have no summer gig and it was hot,

and when it's hot in Paris, you really hot, man.
Things was very bad, so, a fellow named Briggs,
Arthur Briggs, a trumpet player, he was a great trumpet
player.
Where was he from?

He, Arthur Briggs was a New Yorker
but I think originally he was from there.--I mean West Indian--Caribbean person.
So, all right, Briggs got a job for me to entertain at a place called The Paragola--Oostende-- East end.
Right across from Dover. You can see the boat coming in over there at 5:00 o'clock every day.
Englishmen would come to Oostende (phonetic) for their vacations, you see. / The working class people. Now, this place that we were playing in, it was for the rich people, the casino, they had a symphony orchestra and they had us there.
They had a symphony orchestra all the time. That was a big casino. They used to call it the Knokke....., the Casino de Knokke.
So, I got that job to go to Austern. We stayed there and then it got rougher and rougher. And people start to making it home, and where we're coming from but I keep seeing lot of other new people coming in. They didn't seem to be worried at all.
So, all right, I -- I'm playing, and they had a boy by the name of Red DuBoy. (phonetic). He was a saxophone
player.
Red Dubroy?
Red DuBroy. He was from Holland.
How do you -- Dubroy?
No, Red -- it was De Broy, because see, the Dutch people have names like that.

So, he was a nice saxophone player and he had a little girl sing with him called Jope van Deiffe- she was nice, sang nice, pretty little girl too, and then we had a piano player named Gaston. And then the drums, so we had, so I would sing English songs and the people, in unison, everybody would sing and everybody was happy.
So, we were doing good and the money was beautiful. It was lovely.
So, all right. We were getting ready to close August 15, I mean, September 15, they closed and people go to the city.
That night, of August -- was it August or September, I think it was September 2nd, there was a long distance call from Sweden because my Swedish girl was supposed to come down and visit me.

She said, 'I can't get across the frontier, that war has been declared and I can't cross the frontier.' That was it. So I said, well, let them do what they got to do. I wouldn't care less, but the next day, there was a -- I heard

someone calling me.

The fellow was named Pops Foster. He was a comedian and he was an old fellow. He was a comedian and a dancer. and he's hollering Jacques, Jacques -- he had one of them strange voices that could carry but you could hear him.

So, I --
So, he's different from the Pops Foster that --

No, it's not the same one. That's what I wanted to -- and, I went downstairs and he says Man, you'd better get out of here. This is it. And I looked down and they had trenches in front of me. They had trenches and/ every- thing.

I ran upstairs and packed and by the way, she had told me, I'm going to send you a telegram with some money in it and you can come to Sweden. You be away from that war, see. So, I got the money.

Now, but --/ this ship didn't have no room and it was leaving out, and that was the last one going that way. The man says, well, I advise you to go to a place -- go to Dunkirk because the ships are leaving from Dunkirk, going to Denmark and you'll be right.

But there is another place in Belgium, I forget the name of this place, it's right across the bridge from Dunkirk.

So, I said -- and the frontier is closed off see. I was lucky enough to go back and get my -- I said, well, I'll
be in Dunkirk, I might get that ship, even a Dutch ship or a Danish ship.
Got up there and I stayed up there. The Germans come in. They come in there and they stayed there for about -- I mean, they stayed.

Now here's where I said well, if they are going to do me in, I'm going to get pretty I decided -- well, I got my suit on and so, I was -- what do you call the big hotel there -- the Metropole They are saying all this Dutch and, the Dutchland so, they said, all citizens stay in the house.

Queen Wilhamina had said -- because she had, the proclamation that she had surrendered -- she spoken French and all that and what she said, she said, please do not hurt my black population. Don't hurt my black population.

They come in there, and they played "Deutschland uber Alles" (inaudible), and there was hailing and going on, and I was right -- when the big man come out of the car, I was right there so he could see me right there.

Say what?
He went on in, and the soldiers was there standing right on guard there. I said, well, so far so good.
