What year was this you came back?

I came in in '70. And when I got on -- come out and I had an old thing of silver dollars (inaudible) and I kept those silver dollars because they're worth a lot of money. And then I took a taxi and come down 9th Avenue, I said well, look how pretty 9th Avenue is. Then I come across town. I come across town to 2nd Avenue and I got to St. Marks and I saw a man standing there with a sack on his head with two eyes burned out. It was raining and I saw that, and I saw all these characters, people laying out in the street. And you know those beer tops -- beer rings (inaudible).
Off of those pop tops?
Yeah. And then I saw -- I looked at the television and hear about all this crime and mugging, I stayed in the house for two weeks and didn't go out.
Two weeks?

Two weeks. I did not go out. Took me -- I had a hard time. Took me about three weeks to go up to 50th Street. And it took me about six months to go uptown. And that's what happened. And now, I just said, well, Jacques, --yourself for other things. So that's what happened.
So now I've written a whole lot of stuff and I've recorded a lot of stuff, and I'm going to do some more recording.
And then I'm going back to France.
Okay, now, over the last nine years or so in New York, you've stayed in New York the last nine, or have you been going around?
No, I've been to Canada, too.
You've been in Canada?
Oh, yes, I've been to Canada. I've been to Canada. But my domicile is in New York but I would go to Canada some two or three weeks, then I'd come back. Two or three weeks and come back. I did that.

Canada because, see, Canada, it's just too much wear and tear going up and coming back. If you're going to stay about three months, it's good. But if you've got two weeks and you come back (Unintelligible). And especially it seems like your bookings are in the winter time.
Now, did you make any -- one of the things I forgot to ask you, have you made any recordings throughout your career?

I made a lot of recordings in France, see. I made a lot of recordings. I made some in Norway. But I haven't made any here -- it's what I would like to do. I haven't made any yet because, see, when I went to Europe, I was first trumpet player. And I developed into a jazz man over there. So they wouldn't know me. I'm a surprise. I'm a surprise physically, looking at me, mentally, because I've

got all types of things, I'm something special. When I do do what I want to do, they're going to be surprised. They'll say man's coming from every angle, I can't understand where he's coming from. Have you heard some of the stuff I'm doing? So that's what's happening.
Well, I'll tell you, Mr. Butler, it's been -- guess we got it.
Well, indeed.
Quite an experience.
It is. Thank you.
Okay, thank you. Well, Smithsonian, hope you can handle this one.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Copyright notice, Smithsonian header and start of recording
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright notice, the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Project header for cassette 1 (Stanley Crouch, January 27, 1979) and Crouch's spoken opening at Butler's home.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Born in Foggy Bottom, mother's Louisiana family, absent father
segments.summary: Butler was born in Washington in 1909 in Foggy Bottom; his mother was from Lafayette, Louisiana (Lefebvre family, Negro and Indian mix) and he never really knew his father.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Earliest memories: baby carriage, brother's death, being born with a veil
segments.summary: His first memories include reaching for a bird from his carriage, a baby brother who died of diphtheria and scarlet fever, a childhood fall, and his mother's talk of his being born with a veil.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Runaway adventure with little Willie Watson
segments.summary: As a three- or four-year-old he wandered off with a spoiled neighbour boy, Willie Watson, and the two ended up at the police station, where Willie screamed and rolled on the floor until given ice cream.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Kindergarten at Hardicht's Brewery, learning German, the ice house
segments.summary: His mother worked at a German brewery whose kindergarten taught the children German; they pasted labels on bottles and played dangerously in the ice house.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Chores, laundry work and his mother talking to animals
segments.summary: His mother worked two jobs and took in laundry; he learned to cook, sew, scrub and iron ruffled shirts, and watched her talk to dogs and cats as if they understood.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: First hearing a violin and big band; family singing solfeggio
segments.summary: Sent on an errand around age eight or nine, he heard a violin and a band (possibly Ford Dabney's) at a dancing place, and recalls his family singing solfeggio and old French-African songs.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Setting pins at the YMCA and hearing Meyer Davis on crystal sets
segments.summary: Around age ten he set bowling pins at the YMCA in a servile capacity, heard a gifted young pianist there, and was opened up by Meyer Davis's orchestra on early radio.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: The war years and the sick Indian visitor in his mother's house
segments.summary: Asked about World War I, he says he remembers little, but recalls a sick Indian-looking man who stayed three weeks while his mother spoke Creole with him, possibly Parkinson's, and talk of voodoo.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Boyhood clothes, the Buster Brown shoes, and teasing at school
segments.summary: He describes the Norfolk suit, ribbed stockings and heavy shoes every boy wore, his constant runny nose and the hurt of schoolmates saying he smelled, which faded after age seven or eight.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Wanting to be a general; Mr. Dorsey, the White Wing wagon and the draft
segments.summary: At ten he wanted to be a general; he loved riding with Mr. William Dorsey on his street-cleaning wagon, saw omens of pigeons before Dorsey and another relative were drafted, and obeyed his mother absolutely.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Ukulele, Emmy Lucas and working toward a clarinet
segments.summary: At about thirteen he played ukulele and was told by the strict pianist Emmy Lucas to study; he was saving for a clarinet when he was sent to Louisiana on vacation.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: The diving accident, amputation and hopping at the pin alley
segments.summary: A rusty tin cut his leg diving into a wharf in Louisiana and the leg was amputated; mother and son spoke no word for two weeks, and he went back to setting pins on one leg, then bought an artificial limb.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Starting a band with the Walker brothers and Phineas
segments.summary: He began studying clarinet and organised a band with the Walker family and his friend Phineas, rehearsing to the delight of the neighbourhood and a bulldog.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Switching from clarinet to trumpet at Manual School
segments.summary: Because the clarinet lacked the melody he moved to trumpet as his second instrument, played in the Manual School orchestra and won valedictorian honours playing Ave Maria.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Rudolph Eglin and the rival Washington bands
segments.summary: He joined Rudolph Eglin's band, and describes Washington's neighbourhood jazz bands (Sam Taylor's, Cyrus Carter's Jazzhounds) and their tunes, and hearing high-note trumpeter Henry Goodman before he knew Louis Armstrong.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Dunbar and Armstrong Manual: the high-school ROTC drill competitions
segments.summary: He explains the Negro high schools, Dunbar and Armstrong Manual Training, and their uniformed ROTC competitions and the drill teams that won the cup.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: The White Brothers society band, the Bluebirds and the Smart Set
segments.summary: The light-skinned society elite hired the White Brothers; when they could not play, Butler's Bluebirds played the Smart Set dances, which turned away darker guests, who went to Pythian Hall.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Society dance repertoire and reading dynamics
segments.summary: The bands copied Meyer Davis's new pieces and played waltzes like Champagne Waltz, reading the dynamics to shade the sound.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Struggling through high school and Howard; the Howard Theatre audition
segments.summary: Juggling gigs and mathematics he barely finished high school and college sophomore year at Howard; at sixteen he auditioned at the Howard Theatre for Sylvester Lewis and was sent away for being underage.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Losing at dice at the Smart Set Social Club
segments.summary: Paid five dollars for a gig, he gambled upstairs, lost it, was kicked down the stairs by the caretaker and never gambled again.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: Joining King Swayzee at the Mid-City Theatre and leaving on the road
segments.summary: He joined King Swayzee's jazz band as second trumpet, left on tour without telling his mother, played all summer for almost no pay and dropped out of school.

segments.chapter: Washington childhood and first bands
segments.title: King Oliver as described by Swayzee, Lips Page and Louis Metcalfe
segments.summary: Swayzee sounded like King Oliver, and Metcalfe told Butler that Oliver was the master who could play everything and who fired him from the band.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Stranded in Newark, back to the Bluebirds, and the girl with the police dog
segments.summary: The Swayzee band was stranded in Newark; he went home, saved up, returned to Newark for a girl and was frightened off by her dog, then studied with Emory Lucas.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Playing the Big Apple in Newark with Joe Crump
segments.summary: He took a job at a rough Newark club under Joe Crump, a gold-toothed leader who could not read music, across from Joe's bordello, while Butler studied classic harmony and counterpoint.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Living alone above the club and landing the Orpheum Theatre pit job
segments.summary: He lived alone upstairs at the club after the chef attacked the owner, then got a sick trumpeter's chair at the Orpheum Theatre pit and was hired on the spot.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Seminole, Johnny Jones 101 Ranch and bandmaster Edgar Battle
segments.summary: Butler talks of the left-handed pianist/xylophonist Seminole, then of the 101 Ranch show's bandmaster Edgar Battle, and of playing for the New York shows that came through the Newark pit around age eighteen.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: The Newark pit orchestra for silent films
segments.summary: The pit band, led by violinist Floyd Hickman with Ted Nixon on trombone, were virtuosos who played heavy classical music for silent pictures, giving Butler broad experience.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Teaming with Eddie Durham; first approach to Small's Paradise
segments.summary: Butler and Eddie Durham became close, gigging together at dancing schools, then he went to New York and presented himself at Small's Paradise, where June Clark and Teddy Hill were.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: First night in Harlem: Myra Johnson and the strange rooming house
segments.summary: Singer Myra Johnson protected the eighteen-year-old and put him up in a house where he was alone and frightened, and he left after two weeks.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Harlem wonderland: the Rhythm Club and Jelly Roll Morton's audition
segments.summary: Living on Edgecombe Avenue, he haunted the Rhythm Club among Harlem's stars, and Jelly Roll Morton had him read music on the spot and told him to return at eight.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Playing with Jelly Roll Morton: gangsters, bordellos and his sermons
segments.summary: Butler describes Morton berating a singer, gangsters, rushing out the back door, and Morton's contradictory preaching about morals while running bordellos.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Dancing-school gigs and Morton's harmonic knowledge
segments.summary: Butler played dancing schools, and says Morton knew his harmony, was first to put the music on paper, and used simple scales, seventh and ninth chords and occasional diminished.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Cliff Jackson's group, harmony study and syncopated tunes
segments.summary: Working with Washingtonian Cliff Jackson, with Hank Larson on drums, Butler studied harmony and learned new syncopated music such as Louisiana Bobo and Archie Bleyer's writing.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Gershwin's mentor, the old master on St. Nicholas Avenue
segments.summary: Butler tells of an old New Orleans musician on St. Nicholas Avenue (Dave Faulk?) who Gershwin allegedly studied with, his secret polyharmony, and Art Tatum's hidden complexity.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: End of cassette 1 and start of cassette 2
segments.summary: Crouch ends the first side; the Smithsonian header for cassette 2 (January 29, 1979) and proceedings begin.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: A composer's band, Cyril Hunt and Louis Bacon, and Caribbean dance gigs
segments.summary: Butler joined a friend's band with Cyril Hunt and Louis Bacon, played first trumpet, then gigged around including the Caribbean dances at the Renaissance for Happy Andrade.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Studying trumpet with Slossberg
segments.summary: He studied intermittently with Slossberg, teacher of Bunny Berigan, a trumpet virtuoso who adored Armstrong but told him to be himself.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Billy Fowler's Monte Carlo band and learning from Henry Walton
segments.summary: Billy Fowler's professional dance band, newly back from Monte Carlo, was Butler's first big band of pros; trumpeter Henry Walton taught him wisdom if tersely.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Atlantic City and the German restaurant job
segments.summary: The Fowler band played Atlantic City and a classy German restaurant on 59th Street, with repertoire of classics and light music at good pay.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: The crash, Lenox Club and Jack Johnson
segments.summary: After Wall Street crashed Butler took a job in Cliff Jackson's band at the Lenox Club and recalls Fowler's band stranded in Shenandoah, Jack Johnson as band owner and Johnson's advice about using one's head.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: The Lenox Club band under Cliff Jackson and Jeff Blunt
segments.summary: The Lenox Club drew number runners and the Cotton Club's turned-away crowd; the ten-piece band played hard syncopated numbers, with Herb Branch and Edgar Allen on lead trumpet.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Burned out by nightlife; trouble with the horn
segments.summary: Overindulging in romance and late nights, Butler woke one morning unable to get a sound from his trumpet; his doctor said he was just worn out.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: The manager's girl, Jeff Blunt and the dropped music stand
segments.summary: A woman admirer, who was manager Jeff Blunt's girlfriend, forced Butler to her table; when Blunt threatened him he dropped the stand on him, and the bouncer intervened.

segments.chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
segments.title: Kept by a woman: apartment, pistol, tailored suits and a gold horn
segments.summary: She moved him into an apartment with a sunken tub, gave him a pearl-handled automatic and suits, and he recovered his own horn from Blunt, as the Depression arrived.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Depression years and joining Lucky Roberts
segments.summary: As times got rough in 1931-32 Butler joined Lucky Roberts's society orchestra, which demanded classics, the latest numbers and impeccable deportment.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Playing society estates and yachts for Lucky Roberts
segments.summary: The nine-piece band played teas, dances and regattas on millionaires' estates, with members singing, plus anecdotes about a drunk trombonist and Lucky's 'demon' talk.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Leaving Lucky for jazz; Joe Smith, Doc Cheatham, Cuban Bennett, Jabbo Smith
segments.summary: He left Roberts because jazz mattered most after hearing Armstrong, and praises Joe Smith, Doc Cheatham, Cuban Bennett and Jabbo Smith's battle with Armstrong.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Armstrong's foundling-home training and orphanage trumpeters
segments.summary: Butler believes Armstrong learned rudiments and tonguing in the Waif's Home, like other orphanage-trained trumpeters such as Jabbo Smith and Gus Aikens, who knew solfeggio.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Armstrong on the Paris Blues set; the smaller-bore advice
segments.summary: He met Armstrong only when they made Paris Blues together; Armstrong told him to use a smaller bore horn so as not to wear himself out, and Butler recalls the Hot Fives records.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Rex Stewart takes on Armstrong at the Lenox and Rhythm Club
segments.summary: Butler recounts Armstrong's visits to Harlem, Rex Stewart's triumph on Slew Foot Stomp at the Lenox Club, rival trumpeters at the Rhythm Club, and Armstrong's effect at the Lafayette.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Horace Henderson's band; the 1933 Berlin summer contract
segments.summary: Returning in 1929 after Fowler and Roberts, Butler joined Horace Henderson's band, playing his brother's music at college proms and parties at the Dunbar Palace until about 1933-34. He then took a summer contract at the Feminina in Berlin in 1933.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Duke or Fletcher: the best big band of 1928-33
segments.summary: Asked which band was the best, Butler says it was a toss-up between Ellington and Henderson, with Chick Webb also fine.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Meeting Duke Ellington; a shared birthday and temperament
segments.summary: Butler was asked to join Ellington's band but was busy; he says he and Duke share the same sign and manner and understood his music.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson and the aloofness of big stars
segments.summary: He loved Fletcher Henderson but explains how great bandleaders were hard to approach, with sidemen like Sonny Greer as gatekeepers.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Ellington on radio from the Cotton Club and battles of bands at the Savoy
segments.summary: Musicians heard Ellington only on the radio from the Cotton Club until the Savoy Ballroom battles with Henderson, where Tricky Sam growled the St. Louis Blues.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Red Allen's New Orleans delivery and his years with Armstrong
segments.summary: Butler recalls Red Allen's rise with Louis Russell at the Saratoga Club and his soulful solo on You Gave Me Everything But Love, and says he stayed with Armstrong to learn and save his lip.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Bix Beiderbecke's playing within his range
segments.summary: Butler hung out with Bix, who drank gin, and praises him for playing only what he knew and resolving every note, a lesson he links to Slossberg's advice.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Bubber Miley and John Mack's small-cup mouthpiece
segments.summary: He met Bubber Miley and Tricky Sam; he describes the mouthpiece made for Armstrong that raised the trumpet's range and ruined many players' lips.

segments.chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
segments.title: Armstrong returns from Europe and cuts Rex Stewart
segments.summary: Prompted by Rex Stewart's account, Butler says Armstrong, written off while in Europe in 1934, came back with crystallised playing and killed the trumpet section on the first note.

segments.chapter: Berlin and the Turner and Bryant bands
segments.title: Berlin cabaret in 1933: Annie Goudy and Mack the Knife
segments.summary: Back on Berlin, he describes the Feminina with seven bands and singer Annie Goudy singing Mack the Knife, in a style he thinks influenced Piaf, plus Marlene Dietrich or Lotte Lenya.

segments.chapter: Berlin and the Turner and Bryant bands
segments.title: Gene Kennedy and the Million Dollar Ballroom's Mr. Carrigan
segments.summary: Back home he played with Gene Kennedy at the Million Dollar Ballroom on Broadway, run by mirror-lined Mr. Carrigan, with the entertainer Bennett Matthews.

segments.chapter: Berlin and the Turner and Bryant bands
segments.title: Germany in 1933: Hitler, marks and no race problem
segments.summary: Butler says he did not follow politics, just got paid in marks, and met no racial problem in Germany; he joined Charlie Turner's band.

segments.chapter: Berlin and the Turner and Bryant bands
segments.title: Charlie Turner's band, a quarrel with his best friend, and Willy Bryant
segments.summary: His childhood German helped him get by; he left Charlie Turner's band by urgent request after a falling-out and then joined Willy Bryant's happy band.

segments.chapter: Berlin and the Turner and Bryant bands
segments.title: Turner's sidemen, Butler's own singing band and the Kentucky Ballroom broadcast
segments.summary: He lists Turner's personnel (Slick Jones, Hank Jones, Bobby Stark, Eddie Mallory, Garvin Bushell), then his own geechie vocal band which was pulled off the air at the Kentucky Ballroom.

segments.chapter: Berlin and the Turner and Bryant bands
segments.title: Willy Bryant's band, a telegram from Paris, and the Oglethorpe incident
segments.summary: He was happy touring the South with Willy Bryant until a telegram came to join Willy Lewis; in Oglethorpe, Georgia, Bryant drew a switchblade after a girl's remark and the band covered with Sweet Georgia Brown.

segments.chapter: Berlin and the Turner and Bryant bands
segments.title: Band teasing: Long John Silver, Gorilla and 'Master Race'
segments.summary: He describes how big-band musicians needle each other with nicknames and cowbells, and how thin-skinned players quit because of it.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Sailing to Europe in 1936 and starting at the Chez Florence
segments.summary: Butler crossed on the Ile de France in a Teddy Bear coat and joined Willy Lewis at the small Chez Florence in Paris, bringing new Roberta music and the covered tone learned from Henry Walton.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: The bidet
segments.summary: A comic story of Butler's puzzlement at the hotel bidet, finally explained by a lady friend.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Willy Lewis's band: Herman Chittison, Bill Coleman and singing rehearsals
segments.summary: Pianist Herman Chittison, Bill Coleman's absence, and a first month of singing rehearsals of German and French songs under leader Willy Lewis, who advised him to sing like Louis Armstrong.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: The Willy Lewis seasonal circuit and picking up languages
segments.summary: The band wintered in France, spent spring in Egypt and summer at Knokke, Belgium, and Butler used Creole with West Indians to pick up French.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Alexandria: the Greek owner Pastudes, hotel pounds and Stardust
segments.summary: In Alexandria the owner Pastudes treated the band lavishly; Butler took a cheaper room and won over a cold audience with a Stardust solo.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Big Boy Goudie slaps Willy Lewis; the band debates ousting him
segments.summary: Resentful of pay differences, Big Boy Goudie slapped leader Willy Lewis at Thanksgiving dinner and the band discussed the contract consequences.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Chittison, the 'bomb dropper' with telephone numbers
segments.summary: Pianist Chittison writes down numbers of women constantly, and Butler warns him against dropping bombs where he doesn't know people.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Start of cassette 3
segments.summary: Smithsonian header for cassette 3-4, dated January 28, 1979, and Crouch recapping where they stopped.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Tarbooshes in Alexandria and Chittison jailed
segments.summary: The band wore tarbooshes to avoid street hustlers; at the club Chittison dropped a note into a woman's hand, waiters seized him and he was jailed overnight.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Butler's Swedish girlfriend and the jealous doorman with the knife
segments.summary: A girlfriend from Sweden visited, and the hotel doorman chased an Englishman who walked her home; the recording was interrupted and resumed January 29, 1979.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Billy Burns, Pastotis's wife and the Packard
segments.summary: Butler enjoyed camel rides and Egyptian friends; he describes white trombonist Billy Burns's lavish lifestyle and his rivalry with Pastotis over Pastotis's Greek wife and a new Packard.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: A Greek cabaret night out and arrest by the Sudanese police
segments.summary: Chittison took Butler to a Greek cabaret full of German girls, took a woman's pocketbook home, and at dawn a seven-foot Sudanese policeman fetched both men.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Tried by an Egyptian judge; near sentence of hand-cutting
segments.summary: Butler and Chittison were tried in a tent by a judge who mocked their Western clothes; they were nearly sent to the desert but, when the Greek owner vouched for them, were fined and sentenced to pay the woman back.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: A pasha's invitation and harem
segments.summary: A pasha entertained Butler at his home with couscous and showed his harem, urging him to learn Arabic and stay, as Egypt would soon be free of England.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Playing at King Farouk's wedding and leaving for Holland
segments.summary: Before summer the band left Egypt for Holland, having played King Farouk's wedding, and Chittison nearly got jailed again; Wilson Miles was passing himself off as a local.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Amy sings 'Ole Man River' on the ship home
segments.summary: On the ship back, the singer Amy was pressed to sing Ole Man River; when she sang the original lyric's slur everyone fled, leaving Bill Coleman's foster daughter bewildered.

segments.chapter: Willy Lewis band in Paris and Egypt
segments.title: Spending money in Holland and rumors of Hitler
segments.summary: The band arrived in Holland in fezzes with Egyptian spoils, was jailed for spending too fast, played a Dutch engagement and heard rumors about Hitler at the end of 1936 and in 1937.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Back at the Chez Florence among five kings; Paris as entertainment capital
segments.summary: Returning in spring, the band played for kings and royalty at the Chez Florence; Butler describes Paris as the hub of entertainment with Eddie South and Benny Peyton passing through.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Benny Peyton's drumming and playing for European audiences
segments.summary: Drummer-bandleader Benny Peyton, long in Europe, knew how to make audiences understand jazz and was always working, and in Switzerland they wanted spirituals and St. Louis Blues.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Bricktop's, the Cubans and keeping your own style
segments.summary: He lived at the Hotel Rochechouart, describes Bricktop's cabaret and rivalry from Cuban bands, where each played their own music well.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: The Russian troupe, gypsy music and the Montmartre circus
segments.summary: Below his hotel a Russian troupe sang czardas and gypsy music that stuck with him, and nearby were a small circus and Antillean dance halls.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Pigalle's expatriates: Mabel Mercer, Opal Cooper, Juice Wilson
segments.summary: He lists Americans playing in Pigalle, Bricktop's with Mabel Mercer, singer Opal Cooper, Glover Compton, Arthur Lanier and violinist Juice Wilson, who stayed too long in Algeria.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: The Kentucky Singers' spirituals in Paris
segments.summary: Mabel Mercer's sound and the four unaccompanied Kentucky Singers who could set a room on fire with spirituals.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: The Hot Club of France and Django Reinhardt
segments.summary: A gypsy band with Django played at the club while Butler's band rested; Django arrived with relatives some nights, and the French bassist was Vola.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: After-hours jam sessions with Ainkion, Oscar Ellman and Bill Coleman
segments.summary: After work musicians jammed: the Czech saxophonist Ainkion, Alix Combelle, an unnamed trombonist, Bill Coleman, and Argentine guitarist Oscar Ellman; King George loved jazz and asked to hear it.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Germans at the hotel, the Rhineland and deciding to go home in 1938
segments.summary: Butler noticed German guests and an English hanger-on, musicians being called up when Germany marched into the Rhineland, and in 1938 decided to visit his family in New York.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Oscar Ellman, the Argentine guitarist
segments.summary: Ellman was a complete guitarist, aspiring to Segovia's mastery yet able to play jazz, whose stinging notes contrasted with Django's, and who jammed with Bernard Addison.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Big Boy Goudie, the New Orleans reedman
segments.summary: Big Boy Goudie (Francis Goudie) played clarinet, tenor and trumpet and led the band the jammers played in; a born jazzman from New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Robert Mavouzy, the Guadeloupean saxophonist
segments.summary: Mavouzy, from Guadeloupe, was another Charlie Parker who could just hear notes; he played in Butler's band, and Butler recalls the confusion about his being American. Butler then remarks that musicians are jealous of each other, more so now in New York.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Home in New York 1938-39: no Black bands and Harlem poverty
segments.summary: Visiting home he felt Black jazz bands were being blocked out in favour of Goodman and Harry James and saw poverty in Harlem, after becoming Europeanized.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: The Ebony Club and Duke Ellington's job offer
segments.summary: At Al Martin's Ebony Club, Willie Manning said Duke wanted him; Butler declined because of his European contract, and he thinks Duke resented the refusal.

segments.chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
segments.title: Sitting in at the Woodside Hotel with Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Billie Holiday and friends left Butler at the Woodside Hotel's bar on 7th Avenue, where he made Sweets give up the stand and played hard.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Back to Europe, leaving Willy Lewis for Ricco's Creole Band in Norway
segments.summary: When war broke out he left after being insulted by Burns at rehearsal, joined a Cuban band, Ricco's Creole Band, and toured Norway, where he started a small jazz club.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: The trombonist John Degrass and Norwegian ladies
segments.summary: Butler marvels at trombonist John Degrass and drummer Walter Johnson picking up women at a Norwegian hotel while the Cubans quarrelled over them; they left in July 1939.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Arthur Briggs gets him a job at the Ostend casino
segments.summary: Back in Paris with no summer work, trumpeter Arthur Briggs found him a job at the Ostend/Knokke casino, where he sang English songs with Red de Broy's group.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: War declared; trenches, Pops Foster and fleeing toward Dunkirk
segments.summary: In September 1939 his Swedish girlfriend could not cross the border; a comedian Pops Foster warned him, he found trenches outside, raised money and tried to reach a ship at Dunkirk as the Germans arrived.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: The German commandant, the brewery and a ration card
segments.summary: In an occupied Dutch/Belgian hotel he faced the arriving German command, who learned he had picked up German at Chris Hart's brewery in Washington and gave him a ration card.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Singing Sonny Boy for the Germans; Hans Buerman
segments.summary: He sang Sonny Boy and German songs for the officers' club, and a soldier who had heard him play at Knokke as a teenager, Hans Buerman, offered papers.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Buerman's help and the plan to escape north
segments.summary: Buerman warns him after seeing a woman dragged away, and offers to help him reach Sweden, Norway or Canada via Gothenburg and Iceland.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Arriving in Norway on a military plane and the officer's glove slap
segments.summary: Flying to Norway with a German colonel's escort, Butler was refused entry for lack of a visa until the officer slapped the customs man; Crouch presses him to clarify who slapped whom.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Working at Oslo's Metropole Hotel despite the American Consul
segments.summary: He found a singing job at the Metropole Hotel the first night, got no help from the American Consul, and obtained working papers from the German consul, playing for sunk-ship crews.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: The Black Prince of Norway and a jazz chapter
segments.summary: For eleven months he was a big man in Norway, nicknamed the Black Prince, taught audiences to clap and swing, and organised a jazz society with British trumpeter Roland Greenberg.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Denmark concert with Svend Asmussen, Valaida Snow and Freddie Crump
segments.summary: Just before the Germans took Denmark he played a concert at Karpehollen with Svend Asmussen, Leo Mathisen, Roland Smith, Louis Sims, and mentions Valaida Snow and drummer Freddie Crump.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Free passage to New York and the ship that was blown up
segments.summary: He got a free ship passage from Oslo to New York, brought the crew to Harlem, and learned the ship was blown up on its way back with everyone lost.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Draft board at Penn Station
segments.summary: Back in New York he was summoned for the draft, ordered to Pennsylvania Station, and subjected to an exam.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Seeking a Norwegian ship job and the translation
segments.summary: He tried to get work on a Norwegian ship because he spoke the language and knew how to catch Germans by a word, and recalls translating for a Norwegian ship.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Wartime gigs with Cass Carr and Buddy Walker; going to Canada
segments.summary: With friends in the army, he gave up shipyard work for music, played with Cass Carr and Buddy Walker, then made an act and went to Canada for about two years.

segments.chapter: War years: Norway, occupation, return
segments.title: Change of tape and February 1, 1979 session
segments.summary: Crouch changes the tape and announces the fourth session, February 1, 1979.

segments.chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
segments.title: Charlie Christian and Oscar Ellman compared
segments.summary: Butler never heard Charlie Christian live but says Ellman, whom he heard personally, was fantastic and would have excited Christian.

segments.chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
segments.title: Django Reinhardt's economy and jazz as statement, painting or poetry
segments.summary: He describes how Django found notes equal to twenty others, and divides jazz players into those who make statements, babble, paint or are poets like Buck Clayton.

segments.chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
segments.title: Pernod in Paris
segments.summary: He describes how the strong licorice-based Pernod was prepared with water and ice, and was outlawed after the war.

segments.chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
segments.title: Melody Maker headline and the Hawkins-Carter jam at Aikian's club
segments.summary: Butler tells how Coleman Hawkins disliked a Dutch headline about his fall, and of the Czech saxophonist Andre Aikian's club, where Benny Carter pulled out a tenor to irk Hawkins.

segments.chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
segments.title: Hawkins blows Honeysuckle Rose and wins over Pigalle
segments.summary: Hawkins, fortified with cognac, played Honeysuckle Rose until the whole of Pigalle crowded around, and Butler predicted he would surprise America.

segments.chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
segments.title: How Hawkins and Benny Carter make complexity sound natural
segments.summary: Replying to Crouch about Hawkins's early harmonic ideas, Butler says great musicians absorb foundations until the result sounds easy, as Benny Carter's humble mastery does.

segments.chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
segments.title: Racial strain on Black musicians and relief in Europe
segments.summary: Asked about Lester Young, Butler says Black musicians are under constant mental strain from racial headlines, which lifts abroad; some use the freedom to learn and others do not.

segments.chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
segments.title: Lester Young and his intentional shock
segments.summary: Butler first heard Lester on clarinet in Moten's band, discusses Herschel Evans, Chu Berry and Don Byas, and sees Lester as an intentional shocker and individualist younger than Hawkins.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: A summer in Saratoga Springs with Scotty of the Missourians
segments.summary: In late 1941 or 1942 he spent a summer at a mountain resort near Saratoga Springs with the Missourians' Scotty, took up archery, and played to Scottish farmers who liked jazz.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: Walking into Rockhead's in Montreal
segments.summary: He went to Montreal, sat in at Rockhead's Paradise, owned by Jamaican Rufus Rockhead, met Bill Kurzie, and was offered an upstairs band, Rockhead's Rendezvous, with pianist Gertie Waters.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: Freddie Blackburn's family tragedy
segments.summary: Drummer Freddie Blackburn, a Canadian of West Indian and French parentage, survived because he was at the movies when his father killed the family.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: Rockhead refuses Butler as leader; matinee success in full dress
segments.summary: Rockhead insisted a Canadian lead; Butler wrote the music, had the band wear full dress, and the French-language matinee with a French theme song was a hit.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: Freddie's sneaky pete, a union man and the envied suits
segments.summary: Freddie hid a gallon of cheap wine behind his drums, and a union delegate named Huey forced Butler to join the local, while Freddie wanted suits like Butler's.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: The visiting star, a dressing-room razor fight and the anthems
segments.summary: A star and a dancer called Flash fought in the dressing room; when the star demanded God Bless America before the British anthem, Butler calmed disorderly soldiers.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: Canadian pickpockets and the star's demand for Georgia Brown
segments.summary: Butler comments on pickpockets and an English girlfriend, then the star demanded Georgia Brown without music; Butler eventually arranged it and she sang beautifully.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: The army takes the musicians; trombonist Frank Johnston
segments.summary: The army, especially the tank corps with many Indian Canadians such as the Kahnawake trombonist Frank Johnston, was draining Rockhead's of players by 1942-43.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: Freddie Blackburn, the Gene Krupa record and the knife
segments.summary: Freddie drank, played along to a Krupa record, and during a number Bill Kurzie pulled a bowie knife to calm him before both were drafted.

segments.chapter: Canada
segments.title: Bill Kurzie's visit to Harlem and later fate
segments.summary: Kurzie in British shorts was mocked in Harlem and returned to Canada; he later married a Syrian woman, and Butler heard he nearly cut a bouncer's arms off with a razor.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Back in New York 1943-51: Dixieland with Art Hodes, Red Allen fill-ins
segments.summary: Returning in 1943-44 he gigged around New York saving to return to France, worked as a Dixieland trumpeter with Art Hodes and subbed for Red Allen, while bebop was emerging.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Willie Lewis's band fighting in Portugal
segments.summary: Butler had been at Teddy Hill's Minton's, and heard that Willie Lewis's band, working in Portugal's casino, fought among themselves instead of staying out of the war.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Ending the session of February 1
segments.summary: Crouch wraps up the tape because Butler has an appointment and they agree to resume the next morning.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Ex-compatriots' bar and Baron Rosencratz
segments.summary: Resuming February 2, Butler describes musicians returned from Paris who hung out at a bar run by Baron Rosencratz and his reporter wife near Edgecombe Avenue.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Hiring young Bud Powell for a Village Corners gig
segments.summary: Butler heard a baby-faced pianist playing, asked his mother's permission on Convent Place, took Bud Powell on a gig, and decided around 1946-47 to return to Europe.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Why he played Dixieland
segments.summary: Dixieland was comfortable, whiskey-drinking music with good money rather than smoking or shooting music, as bebop musicians then struggled.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Studying with Murray Deutsch; freedom in Dixieland; the stolen trunk
segments.summary: He studied Schillinger and Hindemith-type systems with a teacher and found Dixieland a free place to experiment, and lost his study books when his trunk was stolen in France.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Charlie Parker with Jay McShann and Eddie Barefield
segments.summary: Asked when he first heard Parker, Butler says Parker came with Jay McShann, along with the 'demon' Eddie Barefield.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Hearing Charlie Christian over the BBC
segments.summary: Drunk on champagne and rum in Europe, Butler was sobered by Christian's guitar on the BBC and felt he affected him like Oscar Ellman.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: The Norwegian guitarist Robert Norman
segments.summary: Butler recalls hearing another 'demon' guitarist, Robert Norman, in Norway in the late 1930s.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Charlie Parker drives wildly down 59th Street
segments.summary: Butler first heard Parker live in the 1930s; later Parker took him in his car at 60 mph and ran up on a policeman near Columbus Circle before dropping him at Broadway.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Parker's birthday party and the strings record
segments.summary: At Parker's party Butler drank scotch among guests who forgot manners at the buffet, Parker threw him out in jest, and it was the last time he saw him; he later heard Parker with strings.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Parker meets Earl Bostic at Metcalf's
segments.summary: Butler saw Parker and Earl Bostic open together at Metcalf's place, where Bostic's lightning playing prompted Parker to go to the bar.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Floorshow, Don Byas and the honking tenor battle
segments.summary: Tenor Floorshow won sessions with flip-flops and honking until Don Byas jumped on the floor too and chased him to the bar during Cherokee.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Don Byas back in New York with a bayonet: 'I am him'
segments.summary: Both Byas and Butler were afraid to leave their rooms after returning from France; Byas carried a French bayonet, turned religious, and scattered thieves in Beefsteak Charlie's.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Dizzy and Billy Eckstine's band at Club Sudan
segments.summary: Butler led the relief band at Club Sudan where Eckstine's band of future bebop names tried out chords behind his singing until he threatened to disband.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Why bebop did not become his style: Armstrong and Joe Louis in their prime
segments.summary: Having heard Armstrong in his prime, Butler says bebop came too late for him, comparing it to Joe Louis; he chose to refine what made him king rather than sound like others.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Dizzy as pathfinder; melody, pit jobs and Black players
segments.summary: Dizzy changed the instrument like Hawkins, but followers cannot play melody, and Black musicians are excluded from pit bands and hotel jobs; Butler complains of Fiedler and Lawrence Welk.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Fats Navarro and Dizzy's calculated image
segments.summary: He praises Fats Navarro as lyrical like Armstrong, while Dizzy wants to shock and chose his image, with an Ellington story about picking the right notes.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Roy Eldridge, Shad Collins and staying in your own age
segments.summary: Roy Eldridge and Shad Collins came from his sphere; Butler argues that a man shouldn't try to modernise himself like the young or he will harm his health.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Fats Navarro's big sound and Freddie Hubbard
segments.summary: Navarro had a big sound from his mouthpiece and training, and Butler says Freddie Hubbard plays everyone's style, advising to perfect what one is.

segments.chapter: New York 1943-51: Dixieland and bebop
segments.title: Deciding to leave America: veterans' treatment and the Essex House refusal
segments.summary: Seeing veterans denied jobs and being refused a room at the Essex House until a white companion booked it, he played a Princeton job for Red Allen and left for France.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Postwar France: Coca-Cola, black marketeers and higher rents
segments.summary: On arrival France had changed, with Coca-Cola, black-marketing and inflation, and he took an old hotel room.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Eugene Bullard: Foreign Legion colonel and fighter
segments.summary: Butler describes Gene Bullard, a Georgian who fled after killing men, joined the Foreign Legion, became a World War I ace, and defended Black people from Red Grange.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Bullard and the African with filed teeth
segments.summary: Bullard backed down from a fight with a tall African with sharpened teeth.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Bullard and the Corsican gangster brothers
segments.summary: A drunken young Corsican gangster pursued Bullard with a knife and gun; Bullard killed him with a champagne bottle, returned the body to the brothers, and then fined them.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: End of cassette 4 and start of cassette 5
segments.summary: The tape runs out mid-story and the Smithsonian header for cassette 5 (February 6, 1979) begins.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Sidney Bechet and Mike McKenzie's Paris shoot-out
segments.summary: Bullard told Butler that Bechet and McKenzie argued about a chord in a recording studio and shot at each other in the street, and Bechet went to prison for a year with white hair.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Bechet's trial and Bullard's plea to the judge
segments.summary: Facing the guillotine, Bechet wailed in court until Bullard, in his medals, explained Bechet's superstitions to the judge, who freed both men upon payment of indemnities.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: The French mentality of New Orleans musicians
segments.summary: Answering whether New Orleans men were thuggish, Butler says they have a French mentality, were superstitious, could be thuggish, but only the ones in music are known.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Bechet's Lincoln with hidden weapons
segments.summary: In France the second time, Bechet showed off his new Lincoln, which hid a rifle over the windshield, a carbine, a .45 under the dash and more.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Armstrong is no Uncle Tom: the $500 rebuke
segments.summary: Contradicting the Uncle Tom view of Armstrong and Stepin Fetchit, Butler tells how Armstrong rebuked an impresario rubbing his head for luck by demanding $500.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Filming Paris Blues with Armstrong: the head-out-of-the-train shot
segments.summary: On the train scene Butler stuck his head out ahead of Armstrong; Armstrong silently let him do it three times until he understood the point.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Stepin Fetchit as master of psychology
segments.summary: Butler calls Stepin Fetchit a psychologist who gave white audiences the slow, dumb act and used it to profit, robbing gamblers in his dressing room.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Stepin Fetchit and Muhammad Ali
segments.summary: Butler thinks Fetchit influenced Muhammad Ali's fighting and the Elijah Muhammad circle, recalling an anecdote of Fetchit teaching a lady to dance.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Black people as psychologists under pressure
segments.summary: Oppressed people learn ruses like the coyote or fox, and Black people raised in Europe do not know their enemy, as with one of Butler's sons.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: Gentleman thugs: Benny Carter, Leroy Brown and the subway razor
segments.summary: Refined men like Benny Carter and Leroy Brown can be the worst thugs; Butler tells of a man on the El who cut two sailors' throats after being beaten.

segments.chapter: Bullard, Bechet and race
segments.title: The Harlem race riots of 1933 and 1943
segments.summary: Butler describes LaGuardia calming the riots, looting of pawn shops, police horses slipping on marbles, and how the riots pushed entertainment downtown, starting with the Cotton Club.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Postwar France: American soldiers, Marshall Plan and colonial laws
segments.summary: Europe was changed by American influence, the Marshall Plan, price gouging, and Americans pressing bars to bar Black patrons, which French law forbade.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Back at the Chez Florence, and Cuban Pete the con man
segments.summary: He played again at the Chez Florence, where upstairs parties went on, and worked with an Algerian bandleader calling himself Cuban Pete.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: The Bordeaux wine festival gig and the million francs
segments.summary: At a Bordeaux festival Butler overheard Cuban Pete counting a million francs but offering him ten thousand, and took more money by threatening to tell.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Forming the orchestra at the Cigale in Pigalle
segments.summary: He formed an orchestra at a Pigalle club called La Cigale and stayed about ten years, working summers at a large casino.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: The Cigale repertoire: hard jazz, bop arrangements, beguines
segments.summary: Butler played hard jazz with some bop and New Orleans mixed with beguines and boleros, having bop tunes sent over, and Crouch asks about Parker tunes.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Outdrawing the rival club; Benny Waters and Kansas Fields
segments.summary: Butler's club was full every night while a bop rival across town had no business; his band included multi-instrumentalist Benny Waters and drummer Kansas Fields.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Playing the snail at the Casino de Paris
segments.summary: From 1950 he played the escargot and a policeman in the Casino de Paris show and enjoyed the mannequins and dancers while keeping professionally away from them.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Losing the job to Mr. Varna over a blue Cadillac
segments.summary: Owner Varna, who drove a Kaiser, grew jealous of Butler's Cadillac and avoided giving him the promised orchestra leadership; Butler later returned with a better car.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Power in Pigalle: honorary police and CIA offers
segments.summary: Butler says he could fix working-paper trouble, was given an honorary police status, and twice turned down offers from the CIA, once when Martin Luther King visited.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Mavouzy's jealousy and reputation
segments.summary: After Benny Waters left, saxophonist Robert Mavouzy of Guadeloupe, a brawler in the papers every weekend, was jealous of Butler, a foreigner.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: New Year's Eve full dress and Mavouzy's overplaying
segments.summary: Butler put on full dress at intermission; Mavouzy imitated badly, threatened him, then overplayed Cherokee, and Butler brought the crowd up with Night Train.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Mavouzy starts his own band and it collapses
segments.summary: Mavouzy's rival band on the Grand Boulevard drew people on opening day, but a Jamaican trumpeter cut him with a razor and the audience returned to Butler's.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Bud Powell, Kenny Clarke and Benny Bailey sit in
segments.summary: Bud Powell and Kenny Clarke worked at the Blue Note while Butler held court; Benny Bailey, in Paris with Quincy Jones's band, asked to sit in and ran through Stardust.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Night Train, French waltzes and renewing the crowd
segments.summary: Butler used Night Train, which Crouch says derives from Ellington's Deep South Suite, plus French songs and the Merry Widow waltz to turn the room.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: North African friends and police roundups during the Algerian War
segments.summary: Butler befriended Tunisian Arabs among his customers, signalled them with The Bugle Blues when police vans closed in, and hid a man in the club.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: A Tunisian friend becomes foreign minister; learning Arabic
segments.summary: The man he hid became Tunisia's foreign minister; Butler visited the mosque, learned Arabic, ate couscous with them and was nicknamed 'ram's head' when his son was born.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Black writers in Paris, Sartre and Pigalle versus the Left Bank
segments.summary: Asked about Cesaire, Damas and Senghor, Butler says the Left Bank students were separate from his Pigalle world, though he met Sartre and actors at Club d'Or.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: The boss sells the Cigale; Baldwin and Langston Hughes
segments.summary: By 1966 the boss planned to sell, Butler demanded a share of the profit, and recalls clientele including James Baldwin and Langston Hughes.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Belgian business venture with a millionaire after de Gaulle expelled the Americans
segments.summary: A Belgian millionaire invited Butler to open clubs after de Gaulle's order forced American forces out; the venture failed and the Paris owner complained he was not resting.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Catching the cashier stealing, with the African waiter Baccuse
segments.summary: A cashier was caught stealing by a bright young African waiter who could calculate like a computer, and Butler took back the money.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Geneva band job and a missed share in a highway deal
segments.summary: After the venture failed he took a band to Geneva for two months, met a man proposing a huge Ivory Coast to Dakar highway, did not ask for a share, then decided to come home.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Returning to a decayed New York in 1970
segments.summary: He returned in 1970 and was shocked by crime and decay on the Lower East Side, staying inside for two weeks and taking six months to venture uptown.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Writing, recording plans and trips to Canada
segments.summary: Butler has written and recorded music and plans to go back to France; he keeps his domicile in New York but plays Canada for two or three weeks at a time.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Recordings made in Europe and none yet in America
segments.summary: He recorded a lot in France and some in Norway but none in the US; he sees himself as a surprise because he developed as a jazzman abroad after starting as a first trumpeter.

segments.chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Crouch thanks Butler, calls it quite an experience, and the proceedings end.
